subject: Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2

messages.author: a418d4f76d8f4739
messages.subject: Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2
parts:
Hello,

Apologies in advance for a somewhat imprecise and arm-waving question, but I wanted to throw this out there and see if anyone else is noticing something similar. I've been working on a couple of fairly involved projects in Stan and making great progress, thanks in large part to this wonderful community of Stan developers and fellow users. I had been running RStan 2.8.0 on R version 3.2.2 until yesterday, when I upgraded to RStan 2.8.2 (I missed 2.8.1) and R version 3.2.3. Since upgrading, I am getting much slower runtimes -- around 3x-4x longer than previously. I've reproduced this on two different Windows 7 machines, and no other changes were made to either system.

I realize the simultaneous R and RStan upgrades make this a badly designed "experiment", but here's what I've tried, in various combinations: (1) restarting my R session, (2) rebooting Windows, (3) removing and reinstalling RStan (always from CRAN via install.packages() and following the steps on the RStan Getting Started guide, including setting optimization level -O3), and (4) uninstalling and reinstalling Rtools (version 3.3.0.1959), always making sure to allow the installer to edit the PATH variable. None of this has made a difference to the ultra-slow performance. I have not yet tried reverting to R 3.2.2 and/or RStan 2.8.0, in part because I'm hoping this issue can be resolved and in part because I have the impression that reverting to old versions of RStan is not super straightforward. I'm willing to try either of these options if that's what it takes to diagnose the problem, though. I'm also happy to provide any R session info or other details that may help track this down.

Like I said, mainly I just wanted to see if anyone else was experiencing this, and if anyone has any suggestions.

Many thanks,
EB

messages.subject: Re: Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2
parts:
Quick update: after a bit of fumbling and multiple attempts, I was able to install RStan 2.8.0 from GitHub. This did not fix the slow runtimes. Next I rolled back to R 3.2.2; still no luck. I even tried going back to the last minor version of RStudio, although that upgrade was a few days ago and I didn't notice any performance hit at the time. Still nothing. Finally I uninstalled and reinstalled everything: R 3.2.3, RStudio 0.99.489, Rtools 3.3.0.1959, and finally RStan 2.8.2 (making sure the -O3 flag was set in my Makevars file). None of this helped.

I have no idea what has happened, but somewhere in the process of updating R and/or RStan, it seems like "a switch got flipped" which fresh installations cannot undo. I'm quite certain the update caused this, given that I was able to replicate the behavior I first saw last night on my laptop, on my desktop this morning. A Stan program that, prior to the updates, took ~25 min to run, took ~100 min immediately afterward. The R environment and function call were identical, and no other changes were made to the system.

I'm at wits' end here. If anyone has any thoughts on what could possibly be going on, I'm all ears. FWIW, below is the session info after reinstalling everything.

Thanks,
EB

Okay, I can do this, but the Stan and R code are pretty unwieldy and it would take a lot of work to boil them down to a minimal reproducible example. Also, the only head-to-head timing comparison that I can cite is for the model I'm actually fitting, and of course there's no way to know the seed from any of the pre-update runs. If it would help, I can try something like the 8 schools example and report how long that takes. I did try that earlier today and my sense was that it seemed slower than before, but of course I'm not intimately familiar with how long it "should" take.

Thanks,
EB

It's possible it is something else simple you can fix. I often fail to consider all the possibilities,and some other potential factors not related to STAN itself that occasionally slip my mind when I have a similar issue are;

I made a "minor" change to the code, or the priors that is screwing things up.
The data I'm fitting this time have parameters that are very large, or are near 0, etc.
R settings have been changed to do something funny, or I unset some default parameter that was set in the past that sped things up.
I'm running other programs and/or haven't reset your machine in a while and it's not getting enough RAM allocated. (reset and keep other programs closed.)
I'm machine is running more slowly because of some other change, hardware issue, or a virus, etc.

Cheers,
David

messages.author: a418d4f76d8f4739
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2
parts:
Sorry, I've been away from internet access over the holiday long weekend. Thanks to all who've weighed in.

Bob: I've been running in parallel both before and after this change, and get_cppo_mode() returns "fast" for both previously saved and newly created runs.

David: I am indeed evidently missing something, but whatever it is, I'm pretty sure it's on the R/RStan/RStudio side as opposed to the OS side. As I mentioned in the OP, I got the same behavior on two different machines after doing nothing but those three updates, and the timing is consistent (albeit not identical, of course) across multiple runs with different or identical seeds, despite restarting R and Windows, etc.

Since I can't go back in time (alas), the only controlled comparison I can think of is between a previously saved stanfit object and a new model run with exactly the same model file, inits, and seed (from get_stancode(old_fit), get_inits(old_fit), and get_seeds(old_fit), respectively), and the same runtime arguments. The seeds were the same for all three chains; I'm under the impression that distinct seeds are generated internally, but correct me if I've got this wrong. The Stan and R code, data, and inits are attached. Here's the timing comparison, on a 2.9 GHz quad-core i7 with 16 GB RAM:

before updates

> cbind(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm), total=rowSums(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm)))
        warmup  sample    total
chain:1 349.483 1238.97 1588.453
chain:2 354.452 1239.17 1593.622
chain:3 349.198 1240.84 1590.038

after updates

> cbind(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm), total=rowSums(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm)))
        warmup   sample    total
chain:1 526.599 3687.639 4214.238
chain:2 521.119 3078.829 3599.948
chain:3 566.603 3683.561 4250.164

Like I said, the code is a bit involved and I don't expect anyone to read it in detail. However, I should mention that the plot has thickened: I did the same experiment with a different previously saved model, and in that case I found no consistent difference in timing! That model takes ~3 h to run, and the pre- and post-update timing was not identical, but the differences were minor and inconsistent in direction and could easily be due to differences in system activity, etc. So it seems there is some sort of model x software version interaction going on here.

To be clear, I'm not trying to lay this issue at Stan's doorstep, and I hope I haven't seemed to suggest otherwise. I have no idea what's going on, and it could certainly be some subtle interaction between R and Stan. Maybe this is beyond the purview of the stan-users group, and that's okay. As I said in the OP, I just found it hard to believe that I'm the only one who's seeing this (on two machines), and I wanted to try and compare notes with others.

Thanks,
Eric

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2
parts: I had a similar setup as Eric so I ran the model before, and then upgraded RStudio, R and rstan to match this scenario. I was not able to recreate the differences in timings as posted.

On Monday, December 28, 2015 at 12:36:16 PM UTC-8, Eric Buhle wrote:
Sorry, I've been away from internet access over the holiday long weekend. Thanks to all who've weighed in.

Bob: I've been running in parallel both before and after this change, and get_cppo_mode() returns "fast" for both previously saved and newly created runs.

David: I am indeed evidently missing something, but whatever it is, I'm pretty sure it's on the R/RStan/RStudio side as opposed to the OS side. As I mentioned in the OP, I got the same behavior on two different machines after doing nothing but those three updates, and the timing is consistent (albeit not identical, of course) across multiple runs with different or identical seeds, despite restarting R and Windows, etc.

Since I can't go back in time (alas), the only controlled comparison I can think of is between a previously saved stanfit object and a new model run with exactly the same model file, inits, and seed (from get_stancode(old_fit), get_inits(old_fit), and get_seeds(old_fit), respectively), and the same runtime arguments. The seeds were the same for all three chains; I'm under the impression that distinct seeds are generated internally, but correct me if I've got this wrong. The Stan and R code, data, and inits are attached. Here's the timing comparison, on a 2.9 GHz quad-core i7 with 16 GB RAM:

before updates

> cbind(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm), total=rowSums(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm)))
        warmup  sample    total
chain:1 349.483 1238.97 1588.453
chain:2 354.452 1239.17 1593.622
chain:3 349.198 1240.84 1590.038

after updates

> cbind(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm), total=rowSums(get_elapsed_time(stan.psm)))
        warmup   sample    total
chain:1 526.599 3687.639 4214.238
chain:2 521.119 3078.829 3599.948
chain:3 566.603 3683.561 4250.164

Like I said, the code is a bit involved and I don't expect anyone to read it in detail. However, I should mention that the plot has thickened: I did the same experiment with a different previously saved model, and in that case I found no consistent difference in timing! That model takes ~3 h to run, and the pre- and post-update timing was not identical, but the differences were minor and inconsistent in direction and could easily be due to differences in system activity, etc. So it seems there is some sort of model x software version interaction going on here.

To be clear, I'm not trying to lay this issue at Stan's doorstep, and I hope I haven't seemed to suggest otherwise. I have no idea what's going on, and it could certainly be some subtle interaction between R and Stan. Maybe this is beyond the purview of the stan-users group, and that's okay. As I said in the OP, I just found it hard to believe that I'm the only one who's seeing this (on two machines), and I wanted to try and compare notes with others.

Thanks,
Eric

messages.author: a418d4f76d8f4739
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2
parts:
In case anyone's interested, I finally figured this out. Turns out the problem was that I neglected to call 

Sys.setenv(MAKEFLAGS = "-j4")

before installing RStan. In my defense, I was just following the letter of the instructions on the RStan Getting Started page, which says "For source builds only (which is atypical on Windows and OS X), set the number of processes to use for the build to the number of cores on your machine you want to devote to the build." My install of R is not from source and I'm not building RStan from source, yet evidently this still makes a difference. Lesson learned. Thanks again for everyone's suggestions, and hopefully this thread might save someone else from the same boneheaded and frustrating mistake.

Now back to fitting models!

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dramatically slower runtimes after upgrading to rstan 2.8.2
parts:
On Tuesday, January 5, 2016 at 5:19:54 PM UTC-5, Eric Buhle wrote:
In case anyone's interested, I finally figured this out. Turns out the problem was that I neglected to call 

Sys.setenv(MAKEFLAGS = "-j4")

I'm glad things are working well for you again, but that can't be the solution to the problem you were facing. The -j4 only affects the installation time (by using 4 cores to install it). It doesn't have any effect on the runtime, although you can execute the chains in parallel using as many cores as you want (either by specifying the cores argument when you call stan() or sampling() or by setting options(mc.cores = ?) in advance). So, something else must have caused / solved the slow runtimes, and I hope that it stays solved when you upgrade to 2.9.0 sometime this week.

Ben
